questions.question: What is an Angular service, and how does dependency injection work?
questions.title: Angular Services and Dependency Injection
questions.direct_answer: An Angular service is an injectable class that holds reusable work such as data access, business rules, or shared state. Dependency injection lets a consumer request a token; Angular finds the nearest provider for that token, creates or reuses the configured value, and supplies it to the consumer.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A service is usually an injectable class with a focused non-view responsibility.
A provider tells Angular how to create or obtain a value for a token.
A component requests the dependency through a constructor or `inject()`.
Angular resolves the request through its hierarchical injectors.
`providedIn: 'root'` normally creates one lazy application-wide service instance.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An Angular service is a class used for work that should not be tied to one component's template. Common examples are making API requests, applying business rules, caching reference data, or sharing a small state model. The class is normally marked as injectable so Angular can construct it and resolve its own dependencies.

Dependency injection separates requesting a dependency from creating it. A provider connects a token, often the service class itself, to a value or creation recipe. When a component calls `inject(ProductService)`, Angular asks the component's injector and then its ancestors for a matching provider. The first match supplies an existing value or creates the service according to the provider's scope.

For example, a `ProductService` provided in the root can inject an HTTP client and expose product operations. Several pages can inject `ProductService` without calling `new ProductService()` or knowing how its dependencies are built.

A service is not automatically global. Its lifetime depends on where it is provided. Providing the same class on a component creates a nearer instance for that component subtree, which is useful for isolated state but surprising if the team expects shared data. Dependency injection also supports value, factory, alias, and class providers; interfaces need an `InjectionToken` because TypeScript interfaces do not exist at runtime. The key idea is a token resolved by the nearest provider, not a magic global registry.

sections.title: Tokens, providers, injectors, and service instances
sections.content:
A dependency request begins with a token. Classes can act as tokens because they exist at runtime. Configuration objects or interface-shaped values usually use an `InjectionToken`. A provider records how Angular should satisfy that token: construct a class, return a fixed value, call a factory, or reuse another token.

Injectors form a hierarchy around the application and its component tree. Resolution begins near the consumer. If that injector has no provider, Angular looks upward until it finds one or reaches the top. The provider location therefore controls both visibility and lifetime. A root-provided service is shared through the application injector, while a component provider creates state local to each instance of that component and its descendants.

Suppose two product pages inject a root `ProductService`. Both receive the same service instance and can share its cache. If each page lists `ProductService` in component providers, each page receives a different instance and cache. Neither result is universally right; the required ownership decides the provider scope.

Services should still have narrow responsibilities. A single global service containing every screen's state becomes hard to test and reason about. Dependency injection makes construction replaceable and test-friendly, but it does not replace good boundaries or make mutable shared state safe by itself.

sections.title: Hierarchical dependency resolution
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Consumer[Component requests ProductService] --> Local[Component injector]
  Local -->|provider found| LocalValue[Scoped service instance]
  Local -->|no provider| Parent[Ancestor injectors]
  Parent --> Root[Application injector]
  Root -->|root provider| Shared[Application-wide service instance]
```

questions.question: How do root and component-level providers affect an Angular service's scope?
questions.title: Angular Provider Scopes
questions.direct_answer: A root provider belongs to the application injector and normally supplies one shared instance. A component provider belongs to that component instance's element injector and supplies a separate instance to the component and its descendants, shadowing an ancestor provider for that subtree.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `providedIn: 'root'` makes a service available from the application injector.
A component `providers` array creates a service instance for that component subtree.
Each instance of the provider component gets its own scoped service instance.
The nearest matching provider shadows providers higher in the hierarchy.
Choose scope from who should share the state and when it should be discarded.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Provider scope answers two questions: which consumers can resolve a dependency, and which consumers share its instance. A service with `providedIn: 'root'` is registered with the application environment. Angular normally creates it only when first requested, and consumers that reach that provider share the instance.

A component can instead list a service in its `providers` metadata. Angular then creates that provider in the component's element injector. The component and descendants resolve that nearer instance. A second instance of the same component gets another service instance, and destroying the component destroys its scoped provider with the subtree.

For example, a root `AuthService` is suitable when the whole application needs one login state. A `CheckoutDraft` service can be provided by `CheckoutPage` when each open checkout should own a fresh draft and the state should disappear when that page subtree is destroyed.

A nearer provider shadows an ancestor provider with the same token. This is powerful for isolation and tests, but accidental component providers often explain why two screens do not share expected state. Root scope can create the opposite problem: temporary feature state survives longer and becomes coupled to unrelated screens. Route-level and environment providers add useful middle scopes for larger applications. The correct location is the narrowest injector whose lifetime and consumer set match the data being managed.

sections.title: Service ownership across the injector hierarchy
sections.content:
Imagine an injector tree beside the component tree. The application injector sits near the top. Each component can add an element injector with its own provider records. A request starts at the consuming component and moves upward. The first provider for the requested token wins.

That lookup creates predictable sharing. Two unrelated pages that reach the root provider get the same root service. Two checkout components that each provide `CheckoutDraft` get two drafts. Descendants of one checkout share its local draft because their requests encounter that checkout's provider before the root.

Scope also affects cleanup. A component-scoped service is destroyed with its owning component injector, so it suits short-lived state and resources. Root services normally live until the application is destroyed. This does not mean all services with methods must be root-scoped; lifetime follows ownership, not class size.

Provider placement should be visible in design reviews because a one-line `providers` array can change application behaviour. Avoid providing a root-intended state service again on a leaf component. Conversely, avoid placing every draft and wizard state in the root merely because it is convenient to inject. Tests should verify whether two consumers are meant to receive the same instance or separate ones.

sections.title: Provider locations and service ownership
sections.content:
| Provider location | Shared by | Typical lifetime | Suitable example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Application/root | Consumers that resolve to the root | Application lifetime | authentication state |
| Route/environment | Consumers inside that environment | Route or environment lifetime | feature facade |
| Component | One component instance and descendants | Component subtree lifetime | checkout draft |
| Child component override | That child subtree | Child subtree lifetime | isolated editor state |

questions.question: When can you use `inject()` in Angular, and what is an injection context?
questions.title: Angular Injection Context and inject()
questions.direct_answer: `inject()` can resolve a dependency only while Angular is running code in an injection context, such as a constructor, field initializer, provider factory, or a function run with `runInInjectionContext`. Calling it later in an ordinary method or lifecycle hook has no current injector and fails.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `inject(Token)` reads a dependency from the current injector.
Constructors and field initializers run in an injection context.
Provider and token factories also run in an injection context.
Ordinary event methods and later lifecycle hooks are not injection contexts.
`runInInjectionContext` can run synchronous setup code with a chosen injector.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An injection context is a period of synchronous execution in which Angular has established a current injector. The `inject()` function uses that current injector to resolve a token. Component, directive, and service constructors run in an injection context, as do their field initializers. Provider factories and `InjectionToken` factories are other common contexts.

For example, a component can write `private readonly api = inject(ProductApi)` as a field. Angular evaluates that initializer while constructing the component, so the request is valid. The method can use `this.api` later because the dependency has already been stored.

Calling `inject(ProductApi)` for the first time inside a click handler or `ngOnInit` is invalid: those methods may be invoked after construction, when there is no current injection context. Moving the call into a field initializer or constructor fixes the ownership and timing. A utility that truly needs an explicit context can use `runInInjectionContext(injector, callback)`, but `inject()` must still be called synchronously inside that callback; an `await` does not carry the context forward.

Constructor parameters and `inject()` are both valid dependency-injection styles. `inject()` works naturally in field initializers and helper factories and can infer optional types accurately. It should not be used as a service locator scattered through arbitrary functions. Dependencies remain clearest when they are resolved during creation and stored on the object that owns them.

sections.title: The current injector during object creation
sections.content:
Angular constructs application objects through injector-managed factories. Before a factory creates a component or service, Angular sets the injector that should answer dependency requests. Field initializers and the constructor execute during that factory call, so `inject()` can reach the correct provider hierarchy.

After construction returns, an ordinary method has no implicit current injector. The component still has every dependency it resolved earlier, which is why a click handler should use `this.orders` rather than call `inject(OrdersService)` again. This rule also prevents a method's result from secretly depending on whichever injector happened to invoke it.

A provider factory is another natural context. It can inject lower-level dependencies and assemble a value. `runInInjectionContext` is available when framework-style setup code has an `Injector` and needs to call an injection-aware function. The callback is synchronous with respect to `inject()`; asynchronous continuations need values captured before the first `await`.

The boundary is easy to test: dependency resolution belongs to construction or an explicit factory. Business methods consume stored dependencies. This keeps classes readable, avoids runtime context errors, and makes dependencies visible when a unit test creates or replaces the object.

sections.title: Valid and invalid inject() timing
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Factory[Angular construction factory] --> Context[Current injector is set]
  Context --> Fields[Field initializers call inject]
  Context --> Constructor[Constructor calls inject]
  Context --> Done[Construction completes]
  Done --> Method[Later method or lifecycle hook]
  Method -->|new inject call| Error[No injection context]
  Method -->|stored dependency| Service[Valid service use]
```

sections.title: Dependency resolution during construction
